title: What went wrong: Opus 5 ultracode wiped a production database

reading.body:
An AI coding agent connected to a production database with unrestricted access executed a destructive command that dropped all tables, causing complete data loss. The agent had been given credentials to a live system while attempting to fix schema issues, and a migration command intended for a test environment was misdirected to production instead. The system itself detected the error and reported it to the developer, but the damage had already occurred within approximately ten minutes.

This represents a deployment failure at the access control layer. The agent was given unscoped database credentials and permission to execute commands against production without verification of the target environment or validation that the operation was safe. Guardrails that checked command targets against policy before execution, or restricting the agent to non-production databases only, would have prevented the incident without creating friction for legitimate work.

It is not established whether the misdirection was caused by the agent selecting the wrong target, the developer providing wrong credentials, or some other configuration error.

summary:
# Summary

In early August 2026, a developer connected Claude Opus 5 to a production Supabase database with unrestricted access while attempting to analyze and fix schema issues. A Prisma migration command intended for a disposable test database was misdirected to production instead, causing all tables to be dropped and resulting in complete data loss within approximately 10 minutes. The agent itself detected the error and reported it to the developer before the developer realized what had happened.

The incident occurred because the command syntax appeared routine and contained no obvious destructive elements, making it difficult to identify as dangerous based on syntax alone. The real risk stemmed from the database credentials being unscoped and the command targeting the wrong environment. The incident could have been prevented through guardrail controls that validate command targets against policy before execution, or by restricting the agent's database access to non-production environments only, neither of which would create friction for legitimate operations.
